target: AG1’s claim that dissection is ethically acceptable because over 98% of dissected animals are already dead and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: AG2 objects that this premise is false in substance: classroom dissection animals are not mostly already deceased, because about 99% are caught in the wild. On that view, dissection harms local populations and biodiversity, so the “already dead” argument does not justify the practice.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally valuable because students need real animals to learn anatomy, build skills, and understand biology.
objection: AG2 argues that the educational goals of dissection can be achieved without dead animals, because synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same or better biology outcomes while avoiding harm to animals.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is harmful because animals used are mostly caught in the wild and this causes biodiversity loss.
objection: AG1 rejects the biodiversity-harm premise by saying classroom dissection specimens are overwhelmingly already deceased—over 98%—and that fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so the anti-dissection harm claim does not fit typical classroom practice.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives such as synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same or better than dissection.
objection: AG1 objects that alternatives do not, in general, provide the same learning outcomes as dissecting real specimens, because dissection uniquely requires physical manipulation of anatomical tissue and thereby develops fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and the motivational “aha” effect.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection uniquely provides learning outcomes that alternatives cannot match.
objection: AG2 challenges the assumption that real tissue is necessary for those outcomes, arguing that high-quality synthetic models and simulations can deliver the same core biology objectives, train the relevant observation and manual skills, and even provide similar motivation and “aha” moments.

target: AG1’s overall defense of dissection as a worthwhile educational practice.
objection: AG2 argues that dissection should not be used because it is not required by AP Biology or Next Generation Science Standards, and it is also not necessary for physician training in the U.S. or Canada; since it is optional, the animal-harm costs are unjustified.

target: AG2’s argument that dissection is unjustified because it is not required by standards or medical training.
objection: AG1 responds that not being formally required does not make a method educationally unacceptable; if dissection is a uniquely effective way to build practical, inquiry-oriented biology understanding, it can still be justified even when standards do not mandate it.

target: AG1’s implication that dissection is acceptable whenever it is uniquely effective, even if not required by standards.
objection: AG2 denies that dissection is uniquely effective, insisting that synthetic models and computer simulations can achieve the same or better biology learning outcomes. If alternatives match the outcomes, dissection is not essential and therefore not justified despite not being required.

target: AG2’s claim that non-requirement by standards or medical training makes dissection unjustified.
objection: AG1 argues that the key question is educational value, not whether a method is explicitly required. Dissection should be retained because it provides practical scientific competencies and motivational benefits that make it worthwhile even without a standards mandate.

target: AG1’s assumption that real specimens are educationally essential because only they can produce the needed skills and insight.
objection: AG2 contends that the same fine-motor, hand-eye coordination, and anatomy-to-function skills can be developed with realistic synthetic models or replicas, and that motivation and “aha” learning can also come from simulations. Therefore, the educational benefits do not depend on killing animals.
